statement: The delegation section also covers the Kafka essentials: everything you should know about Kafka in order to design systems.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: now here I'll cover basically Kafka essentials, which everything that you should know about Kafka in order to design systems

statement: Delegation is the most underrated way to get performance out of a system.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it's like it's the most underrated way to get performance out of system

statement: In a 2020 talk (at the start of the lockdown), a VP of Engineering at Hotstar described the principle Hotstar lives by to handle massive scale on its API side.
detail: The teacher could not recall the speaker's name. He credits Akamai (CDN) more than Hotstar for Hotstar's scale overall, but says Hotstar does the API side well.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: there was a session by VP engineering Hotstar. What he said stuck with me.

statement: Much of Hotstar's ability to handle massive scale is credited to Akamai rather than Hotstar itself, though Hotstar handles the API side well.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Obviously I give credit more to Akamai than Hotstar, but still Hotstar does that pretty well on the API side.

statement: Whatever does not need to be done in real time should not be done in real time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: whatever that does not need to be done in real time should not be done in real time

statement: 'Real time' here means within the context of the request: of everything a request has to do, only what is essential must be done in the request context; everything else is delegated to a worker.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: what is extremely essential for it to do in the request context, do that. For everything else, just delegate it to the worker.

statement: Because the work done inside the request context is bare minimum, delegation gives very fast responses and a good user experience, puts very little load on the database, and lets everything else happen asynchronously.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You get very fast responses to the user. User gets good experience. There is very less load on the database

statement: Leveraging delegation to the fullest is what makes building systems at scale work well.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this is what is superb about building systems at scale, doing or leveraging delegation to the fullest.

statement: Medium example: to show how many essays a user has written, add a `total_blogs` field to the users table and increment it (count++) every time a blog is published.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I can actually add a field in my users table called total blogs.

statement: The same count could be computed with a join; the total_blogs counter use case is deliberately manufactured to explain delegation and lead into Kafka essentials.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you may say, yeah, I can do it with join. Yeah, you can do it with join, but I'm just manufacturing this use case

statement: Incrementing total_blogs is not a critical update, so it can be done asynchronously; that is what delegation is about.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this is not so critical application or not the critical update. I can do it asynchronously.

statement: Core delegation flow: client sends a request; the API server submits a task and sends the response (that is its only job); the task goes into a buffer called a broker; a set of workers consume from the broker, do the heavy lifting, and update the database.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Client, you get a request, API server submits a task and sends the response. That's only the job of API server.

statement: The request context ends as soon as the client gets the response.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Here the request context ends as soon as the client gets the response

statement: The buffer that tasks are submitted to is typically called a broker (message broker / message stream: the same concept here).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it is submitted in a buffer, typically called as a broker, right? Message broker, message stream, same concepts over here.

statement: Medium total_blogs flow: user publishes a blog -> API server puts an 'on publish' message into a broker (e.g. SQS or RabbitMQ) -> a worker reads it and runs its business logic, firing an UPDATE query that does total_blogs++ -> later page reads show the updated count.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Worker has the business logic to do total blog plus plus in the database by firing an update query.

statement: Because the update is asynchronous, the user sees the updated count on their next read/page refresh, not immediately.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the updation is done in an asynchronous way in the database. So whenever a user reads the next time would see the updated value.

statement: Delegation trades a processing delay (from the asynchronous flow) for no synchronous write load on the database: the API server doesn't write directly, there are fewer concurrent writes, and the database experiences less load.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Here you can very clearly see the delay in processing ... So there is no synchronous load on the database.

statement: The database is the most brittle component of your infrastructure; protect it, because if it goes down everything is done.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: database is happy because it is the most brittle component of your infrastructure. Protect it.

statement: Treat your database like a newly purchased, expensive iPhone (or a pampered child): put a nice cover on it, take great care of it, and put as little load on it as possible so it works fine.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: your database is iPhone. You have to take care of it very much because if this goes down everything is done

statement: The broker is the heart and soul of delegation as a principle.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This broker, this is the heart and soul of delegation as a principle.

statement: There are two kinds of broker: message queues and message streams.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: two kinds of broker. First are message queues. Second are message streams.

statement: A message queue is a literal queue into which messages are put; a set of consumers consume messages from it, and these consumers are homogeneous (they all do the exact same thing).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: message queues are literal queues in which you put the message. ... this consumers are homogeneous consumers

statement: Tasks pushed to a queue can be things like: spin up an EC2 instance, update the count, send an email notification, send a reminder.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: spin up an EC2 instance, or update the account, or do or send an email notification, send a reminder
flags: "update the account" likely means "update the count"

statement: SQS and RabbitMQ are message queues.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: SQS, RabbitMQ are queues.

statement: Consumers pull messages from the queue; it is (almost) never push-based, with very few instances of push-based consumption.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the consumer pulls the message from the queue. It's never push base. It's very few instances where you do push base things.

statement: Queue walkthrough: messages are enqueued one after another; consumer 2 pulls first and gets message 1, consumer 1 gets message 2, consumer 3 gets message 3; each processes (does the heavy lifting) and then deletes the message from the broker.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now the third message goes to consumer three. They all do the processing and discard or basically delete the message from the broker

statement: The message queue acts as a buffer holding messages while consumers read and process them, doing the heavy lifting.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Message queue is acting as a buffer for us to keep the message while consumer is the one that is reading from it and processing

statement: When a message is read from a queue it is read exclusively by one consumer; it will not go to any other consumer. All consumers listen to the same queue and run the same business logic.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When a message is read from a queue, it is exclusively read for a particular consumer.
flags: teacher misspeaks: 'It doesn't mean this message will not go to consumer two' — intended meaning is it will NOT go to others

statement: Kafka and Kinesis are message streams.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: another type of brokers called message streams, which is where Kafka and Kinesis fits into the scheme of things

statement: Medium extension: on blog publish, besides count++, we also want to index the blog in Elasticsearch so the search service can use it. One way: the same SQS worker does both the DB UPDATE (count++) and writes the Elasticsearch index entry.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this worker is doing two things. First, it is doing count++ ... And second, it is updating the Elasticsearch

statement: If one worker codebase is shared by two teams (backend/analytics and search), you get people/management problems: fights, one team's changes blocking the other's deployment, uncommitted changes, messy branches, inconsistent code.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You know what happens when you collaborate with other teams? Fights. Changes of one, stops the deployment of others

statement: Failure scenario: the worker does count++ (74 -> 75) but crashes before indexing in Elasticsearch, leaving the count at 75 while search has 74: inconsistency.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: My count says 75, but my search is 74. Problem.

statement: If you retry by reconsuming the message, count++ runs again (75 -> 76) while indexing now succeeds (75 entries), so count says 76 but search has 75: still inconsistent.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So now you have 75 entries over here, but your count says 76. Problem.

statement: Doing two things in one shot is always a problem in a distributed system, because machines can go down, and distributed transactions are extremely costly.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: doing two things in one shot is always a problem in distributed system ... And distributed transactions are extremely costly.

statement: Message streams (Kafka, Kinesis) are the solution to this problem; they work on a different principle from a message queue.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is where message streams came into the picture. ... these work on a different principle.

statement: Message queue = homogeneous consumers; message stream = heterogeneous consumers (e.g., an analytics/backend consumer doing count++ and a search consumer indexing into Elasticsearch, both reading the same messages).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: message queue is where you have homogeneous consumers, where you have message streams, where you have heterogeneous consumers

statement: In a stream like Kafka, messages are buffered until the retention period is over.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: They are buffered in Kafka until the retention is over.

statement: With queues, consumers read, process and delete messages; with streams, messages are not pulled out: consumers iterate over the messages, and no consumer deletes them.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: with message streams, the messages are not pulled out, but rather visually the consumers are iterating over these messages

statement: Messages in a stream stay until the deletion (retention) policy kicks in, e.g. delete after 40, 60 or 100 days, which is up to you; consumers never explicitly delete them.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Deletion policy is deleted message after 40 days or 40 days or 60 days or 100 days. That's up to you.

statement: Each consumer type iterates over the stream at its own pace and does its own thing; the search and analytics consumers don't need to process the same message at the same time.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: These consumers, they iterate over these messages at their own sweet pace and do the own sweet thing.

statement: Because consumer types are independent, if the search cluster / Elasticsearch is down, the analytics consumer keeps processing and moving ahead.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: even if search cluster [unclear], Elasticsearch is down, analytics they has nothing to do with it. It can continue processing

statement: Message streams (Kafka, Kinesis) are the most powerful technology in day-to-day engineering; they have made companies re-architect their whole architecture because they solve massive enterprise problems, partly because managing people is hard.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Kafka, Kinesis, they have worked wonders. ... they have made companies re-architect their entire architecture

statement: With Kafka in Medium: on blog publish a message is sent to and persisted in Kafka; the search service and the counter service (count++ in DB) each consume at their own pace. Each team owns its own codebase: people, manager and organization happy.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Search team owns the search code base, counter service team owns their own code base. People happy, manager happy, organization happy.

statement: Decouple as much as possible.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: do decoupling as much as possible.

statement: Kafka is the backbone of modern computing systems, so you need to know its most critical parts; there are many misconceptions about it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Given that Kafka is the backbone of our modern computing system, we need to know the most critical parts of it.

statement: Kafka is a message stream, not a message queue; messages are persisted almost forever, as per the deletion policy.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Kafka is a message stream in which the messages are persisted almost forever as per the deletion policy.

statement: Kafka has topics (think of a topic like a queue). A message is pushed to Kafka for a particular topic, e.g. 'on publish' (blog published), and stored under that topic.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Internally Kafka has topics. ... Let's say blog published or on publish is one topic of Kafka. So think of it like a queue.

statement: Every Kafka topic has some number of partitions, and different topics can have different numbers of partitions (the board shows 3 partitions of the on-publish topic as blue lines).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: every topic in Kafka has some number of partitions and every topic can have different number of partitions

statement: When pushing a message to a topic you provide a partitioning key; Kafka hashes the key to decide which partition stores the message.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You provide that this is my partitioning key. Depending on the partitioning key ... the messages will be stored in a particular partition

statement: If user_id is the partition key, all blogs published by a given user always go to the same partition (user_id is hashed to pick one of the 3 partitions).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So all the blogs published by a particular user will always go to a particular partition.

statement: You can have one consumer, but typically you run multiple consumers of the same type (e.g. 3 search consumers) to do the work (search indexing) as fast as possible, while counter consumers iterate the same topic independently.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I can have one consumer, but I typically have multiple consumers to do search indexing as fast as possible.

statement: A set of consumers of the same type reading a topic together is called a consumer group in Kafka; Kafka itself handles assigning partitions to them, you don't have to do anything.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this is handled by Kafka. You don't have to do anything. ... this is called as a consumer group in Kafka.

statement: With 3 partitions and 3 consumers in a group: consumer 1 reads partition 1, consumer 2 reads partition 2, consumer 3 reads partition 3.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Consumer one will read from partition one, consumer two will read from partition two, consumer three will read from partition three.

statement: Kafka guarantees ordering only within a partition, not across partitions of a topic: if a user publishes blog 1 then blog 2 (same partition), the consumer of that partition reads blog 1 first; across partitions there are no guarantees.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So ordering guarantees are within partition, not across topic. ... But across partition, no guarantees.

statement: If you add a 4th and 5th consumer to a group reading a 3-partition topic, they get no messages.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: when consumer four starts and consumer five starts, they would not get any messages.

statement: The biggest limitation of Kafka is its parallelism: consumption parallelism depends on the number of partitions of the topic. With 3 partitions you can have at most 3 consumers per consumer type.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the biggest limitation of Kafka is its parallelism. The parallelism of your consumption depends on the number of partitions of a topic.

statement: You can have N different consumer types (analytics, counter, backend, ...) on one topic, and the at-most-partitions limit applies to each type separately.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I can have N different types of consumers ... But for each of them, I can have at max three

statement: You can have fewer consumers than partitions; with a single consumer it gets messages from all 3 partitions, iterating over them in a round-robin way.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if I only have one consumer, then it will get messages from all these three partitions ... in a round robin way.

statement: Committing: after reading some messages, a consumer issues a commit to Kafka; Kafka tracks, per consumer group, the point up to which messages have been read, and the consumer resumes from that point.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: there is a thing called committing after you read a particular number of messages ... Kafka will keep a track of that

statement: If the consumer (not Kafka) crashes after processing 4 messages but before committing, on resume it starts again from the last committed point, so those messages are re-consumed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: before committing my consumer crashed off ... because I last committed over here, so when my consumer will resume
flags: sentence trails off at 01:28:46; 'start from the last commit' implied

statement: Kafka guarantees at-least-once semantics, not exactly-once, out of the box. It has started providing some kind of exactly-once, but it is still not truly exactly-once; there are other ways to achieve exactly-once.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Kafka does not guarantee exactly once semantics. Kafka guarantees at least once semantics.

statement: As a simplistic view, your consumers should be okay with re-consuming the same set of messages again.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: should be okay for you to reconsume ... the same set of messages again. You should be okay with that.

statement: Everything about Kafka here holds for Kinesis too: Kafka has partitions, Kinesis has shards: same thing, different terminology, nearly the same underlying architecture; all message streams operate this way, differing only in API and nomenclature.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Kafka has partitions, Kinesis has shards. Same thing, different terminology

statement: Kafka will be used in almost all the (consumer) systems designed in the course; whenever we delegate and need multiple types of consumers, Kafka is the default choice.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: whenever we're delegating and we need multiple types of consumers, Kafka is, will be our default choice.

statement: There is one place where Kafka does not suit (fails miserably, the worst choice); it will be discussed in a later week.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: there is one place where Kafka doesn't suit, and we'll talk about it in week...

statement: Kafka (and consistent hashing) are not magical solutions to sprinkle like salt into every system; both are very stupid solutions in some cases. Know their strengths and weaknesses to make a sane choice.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Consistent hashing. Very stupid solution in some cases. Kafka, very stupid solution in some cases. They are not magical solutions.

statement: Q: since messages are scattered across partitions, how do consumers in a group coordinate ordering? A: they don't: there is no global ordering in Kafka.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: I said there is no global ordering. That's what I said.

statement: Q: if a consumer subscribes to partition 1, how does it learn about messages in partitions 2 and 3? A: you never subscribe a consumer to only one partition; with fewer consumers than partitions Kafka distributes round-robin (a single consumer gets messages from all partitions). Ideal is N consumers for N partitions, but fewer is fine; still no global ordering.
detail: Student's premise (read somewhere that each consumer in a group subscribes to a single partition and must learn about other partitions) was corrected.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: It is never that you specify you subscribe to only one partition over here. ... if there are N partitions, have N consumers

statement: Ideally have as many consumers as partitions (N partitions -> N consumers).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if there are N partitions, have N consumers, that's the ideal way to build that system

statement: Queues and streams share the basics: both are a buffer holding messages, with consumers that go over the messages and consume them at their own time.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: It's a buffer where you are holding up messages and then consuming at your own sweet time.

statement: Use a queue when you have only one operation (one kind of processing) to do on each message; teacher: 'That's the best way to look at it.'
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: So does that mean if the place where I should use queues is where I have only one operation to operate on? Correct.

statement: Why not always use streams? Cost: AWS SQS bills per message, while Kinesis bills for the duration it is running (infrastructure constantly running). For smaller workloads, go for SQS rather than waste money on streams.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: SQS, AWS SQS bills you per message. Kinesis bills you for the duration that it is running.
flags: check: "So why don't we use streams?" may be a student question

statement: Always think about cost: you are there to save cost for the organization; however fancy a design, if it is not cost efficient it will not see the light of day.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You can design as fancy of a system, but if it is not cost efficient, it will not see the light of the day.

statement: Q: more or fewer partitions? A: it depends on the concurrency / consumption speed you need; add more partitions depending on the expected consumption rate.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: depending on the consumption rate that you expect, you can add more partitions to that.

statement: You can commit after every message, but it's too much; batch commits are better, to avoid a network call for every commit.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: We can commit at each message, but it's like too much. Like, but it's better to do batch commit.

statement: Q: can a message queue have more than one consumer group? A: a queue has one group of homogeneous consumers, whoever reads a message gets it; if you need more than one consumer group, the solution is a message stream.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: Suppose if there are more than one consumer group, then the solution is message stream, not message. Correct. Correct.

statement: Q: if a consumer fails mid-processing, do you manually replay? A: no, retries are a guarantee of the underlying queue. SQS has a visibility timeout: if the consumer fails before deleting the message, after the timeout (typically 2 or 10 minutes) the message reappears at the front of the queue.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: called as a visibility timeout in SQS ... after 10 minutes, the message would reappear at the front of the queue.
flags: check: sentence breaks off at ~01:35:41, words possibly lost

statement: Different queues provide different guarantees (SQS provides different guarantees from RabbitMQ).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: SQS provides different guarantees, RabbitMQ provides different

statement: Not deleting the message is the indication of failure; the consumer must delete the message after processing, and you have to write that in your code.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: You don't delete it. That's the indication of failure. The consumer after processing the message has to delete the message.

statement: In a queue you delete; in a stream you commit. In a stream, if you don't commit, you start again from the last checkpoint.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Queue mein you delete. Okay. Stream mein, if you don't commit, you would again start from the last checkpoint.

statement: Commits are never magical: either you commit on every message in code, or you configure auto-commit or periodic commit. A student who thought commits were internal was corrected.
detail: Student 2 claimed they use streams without writing commit code; teacher: you commit, or you have set auto/periodic commit.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: Either you have to have said commit on every message, as an auto commit or a periodic commit.

statement: Q: is the wait queue for connections beyond the connection-pool limit also a queue? A: two very different things: that is an in-memory queue (queue data structure) inside a process, while a message broker is an infrastructure queue component, a separate process you spin up.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: This is infrastructure queue. This is a separate process that is an in-memory queue.

statement: After the break the class covers concurrency (a small part, with more time next week) and communication (more in depth); all remaining questions are taken at the end and the session doesn't end until all are answered.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: concurrency is a small part, we'll spend more time on concurrency next week, but we'll talk about communication a little more in depth

statement: Concurrency helps you get the most out of a single machine (server, database, async worker) by running multiple processes or multiple threads; multiprocessing and multithreading fall under concurrency.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it helps you extract the most out of your single machine, be it your server, be it your database, be it your asynchronous worker

statement: Concurrency brings issues: communicating between threads/processes (e.g. 'I'm done with this, don't reprocess it') and preventing concurrent use of shared resources.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: How do you prevent concurrent use of shared resources?

statement: Classic race: a global `int count = 0` with two threads each doing count++ 1000 times should give 2000, but you get something like 1997, because count++ is not atomic / not thread-safe.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: my total count should be 2000, but it is 1997. Why? Because count plus plus is not atomic

statement: If you are not from a CS background, do a Google search on why count++ is not thread-safe.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Why? Just a Google search in case you are not from CS.

statement: Concurrent systems are extremely difficult to build because they must guarantee two things: data correctness (the final count must be 2000, not 1997) and high throughput.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you need to guarantee two things. First is to ensure data correctness ... Second is you need to have high throughput.

statement: Locks are a way to ensure correctness: they protect the critical section. Kinds include optimistic and pessimistic locking.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: locks are the way through which you can protect your critical section.

statement: Optimistic and pessimistic locking will be covered in depth in coming weeks (third to sixth); this is just a gist.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we'll talk about them detail in coming weeks, third, fourth, fifth, sixth

statement: Classic implementation: wrap count++ with a semaphore so only one thread at a time enters the count++ while every other thread waits.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you wrap your count plus plus with semaphores and say that at any point in time, only one would move in

statement: Pessimistic locking / semaphores are like traffic signals at a square: the middle of the junction is the critical section (shared resource); one road's signal turns green at a time to use it, then red while another turns green.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The center part of the road is the critical section. At any point in time one traffic signal goes green

statement: Pessimistic locking: lock out other threads while one accesses the shared resource; when it is done, give the next thread its chance.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You are locking other threads while one is accessing it. ... This is exactly what pessimistic locking is.

statement: Computer science concepts can be seen in action in the real world; they are heavily inspired by how humans behave.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You can see them in action in your real world. It's heavily inspired on how humans behave.

statement: Pessimistic locking is implemented with mutexes and semaphores.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: A way to implement pessimistic locking is with mutex and semaphores.

statement: Lock-free data structures exist, such as CRDTs ('the most brilliant data structures'); they won't be covered (advanced data structures), but know they exist.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: there are lock-free data structures like CRDTs, the most brilliant data structures

statement: Concurrency will be covered in high depth in the context of databases, where it will be seen in action.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we'll touch upon this concurrency in very high depth when it comes to database

statement: Medium example: two people clap on an article at the exact same time; if it was 100 it must become 102, not 101.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: two people clapped on an article at the exact same time. ... If it was 100, it becomes 102. It cannot be 101.
flags: asr: [?increment that count | asr: "enter that account"]

statement: Ensure correctness of such updates using database transactions (ACID properties) or, if not transactions, the database's atomic operations.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You do it by using transactions or atomic instructions on your database.

statement: Next week covers database transactions and locking in depth (correctness while keeping high throughput); concurrency also comes in weeks 3, 6 and 7.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Next week, we'll go in depth of database transactions, locking ... we are going in depth in third week, sixth week and seventh week.

statement: Communication is the most neglected part of system design: people just expose a REST endpoint, but that is not the only way.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this is the most neglected part per se, when it comes to system design.

statement: Exposing an HTTP endpoint does not mean it is REST. REST is a specification for how you should expose endpoints; HTTP is a medium/way to implement REST.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: exposing HTTP endpoint does not mean it's a REST call, hundred percent. ... HTTP is a way to implement REST.

statement: The teacher's YouTube video titled "So you know REST?" explains what REST actually is versus HTTP endpoints.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: go on my YouTube channel, you'll find a video titled "So you know REST?"

statement: Remote procedure call (RPC) is the generic term for a client invoking a procedure on a server through a specification; an everyday HTTP web server is one way to do RPC: the server maps a request's format to the method to call.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: RPCs is a generic name, which means that a client can invoke a procedure on a server through a specification.

statement: Standard request-response: the client sends a request, the server does the heavy lifting (database access, computation, encryption/decryption, authentication, authorization) and sends the response. It is the most common communication pattern.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you send a request, server does the processing and sends the response.

statement: Request-response is like ordering a burger in a restaurant: you (client) ask; the kitchen (server) does the heavy lifting and brings it to you.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's like you ordering in a restaurant. You just say, hey, I want burger. The kitchen staff goes and does the heavy lifting.

statement: Short polling: the client repeatedly, periodically requests the server to check whether something is done / what the current status is. It's a way to build a user experience.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: your client typically makes those requests again and again, periodically to the server to see if the things are done or not

statement: Short polling example: launching an EC2 instance in the AWS console shows 'in progress' and changes to 'ready' without you refreshing, because the frontend polls.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now, without even you refreshing, the interface changed from in progress to ready

statement: Short polling is typically used for long-running jobs; it does from JavaScript exactly what the user would do by repeatedly hitting refresh.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: your user hitting refresh again and again versus you doing it on JavaScript is the exact same thing

statement: Short polling example: live cricket scores on Cricbuzz or ESPNcricinfo auto-refresh while a match is live.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: To see the cricket score you go to Cricbuzz or ESPNcricinfo something like that. When match is live it keeps on auto refreshing

statement: Short polling is the simplest, extremely simple way to build this.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is extremely simple to build.

statement: With a 10-second polling interval, each client makes 6 requests a minute; with a million concurrent users that is 6 million requests per minute on the server.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: every 10 seconds you are making one request ... 6 million concurrent requests per minute on server.

statement: Each short-poll is a full HTTP request: connect (three-way handshake), one request, one response, teardown, so there is a lot of HTTP overhead.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: sends a request, gets the response, terminates the connection, so three-way handshake, two-way teardown
flags: teacher says 'two-way teardown'; standard TCP teardown is a four-way exchange — left for fact-checker

statement: Short polling's worst part: the response often doesn't change, e.g. an EC2 instance taking an hour means an hour of requests returning the same redundant status. Disadvantage: the server must handle a huge number of requests.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The worst part is, what if the response doesn't change from the server?

statement: Long polling: the client makes a request that the server does not answer until the state changes (something new to share). Example: after the EC2 launch request is acknowledged, the status request isn't answered until the instance is ready.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this call would not return unless the state changes

statement: No one gives you long polling (or short polling) out of the box; you must implement it yourself, specific to the use case (EC2, cricket score, messaging app), there is no one global way.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: There's not a magical solution that would implement short polling or long polling for you.

statement: Long polling drastically reduces the number of HTTP requests, but someone (the server) has to loop to check whether the state changed; the client makes fewer requests while the server does more heavy lifting than with short polling.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you make fewer requests when you're using long polling, but your server has to do a lot more heavy lifting

statement: Long polling for cricket: a request for the latest score is answered only when the next ball is bowled; the backend runs a loop (expensive) checking for the next ball.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I would get the score only when the next ball is bowled. ... You apply the infinite loop in the backend

statement: Short polling immediately gets a response with the current status (even if 'in progress'); long polling makes the server wait until something changes before responding.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: short polling, it immediately gets a response ... long polling waits, like makes a server wait

statement: WebSockets are the most common way to build messaging apps / real-time communication.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Another one is WebSockets, the most common one that is used to build messaging apps.

statement: WebSockets are like the connection pool from the previous class: an established connection avoids the overhead of re-establishing and terminating TCP connections.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: The concept of WebSocket is very similar to what we talked about yesterday as connection pool.

statement: A WebSocket is a bidirectional channel between the client (end user: browser, mobile device) and the backend server: a persistent TCP connection that understands the WebSocket (WS) protocol.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: WebSockets are bi-directional channel that is established between your client and the server.

statement: Like HTTPS is HTTP with SSL, WSS is secure WebSocket. WebSocket does not run on top of HTTP; it is parallel to HTTP, a different specification.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: WSS is the secure WebSocket. So WebSocket is not running on top of HTTP. WebSocket is in parallel of HTTP.

statement: Because the connection stays open, either side can send: the server can proactively push a message to the client, not just respond to requests.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Here with WebSocket server can also proactively send message to the client.

statement: Chat apps: all clients are connected to the server; when a user sends a message the server immediately pushes it to the recipient, who never has to ask 'any new messages for me?'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When a user sends a message, comes to the server and server immediately sends it to another user

statement: Because they are persistent connections, WebSockets are very expensive to manage.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: because it's a persistent connection, very expensive to manage, very expensive.

statement: Next week (Sunday) covers scaling WebSockets in depth and building Slack's real-time communication.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Next week, Sunday will go in depth of scaling WebSockets, how to use it, how to scale it, how to build real-time Slack communication

statement: Since the connection is already open, any to-and-fro happens at lightning speed (no re-establishing), which is why WebSockets are used for real-time, low-latency data transfer.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: any to and fro that happens, it happens at a lightning fast speed

statement: Stock market tickers (Groww, Robinhood) show prices ticking every second without refreshing because the server proactively sends data.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: stock market ticker, brilliant example. Groww, any app that you use, or Robinhood

statement: Other WebSocket uses: live experiences, multiplayer games, and Zoom chat (messages reach the people connected immediately; those not connected miss them).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the Zoom chat that we use. Zoom chat works on top of WebSockets.

statement: Multiplayer games may use a WebSocket variant; MQTT is a kind of WebSocket equivalent.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you may have heard of MQTT, which is kind of WebSocket equivalent.

statement: MQTT, WebSocket and HTTP are specifications; underneath they must run on TCP or UDP, and a persistent connection has to be TCP. How lightweight it is depends on the spec you use on top.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: MQTT, WebSocket, HTTP, they are specifications. Underlying it has to be either TCP or UDP. Even it is persistent, it has to be TCP
flags: "Even it is persistent" likely 'If it is persistent'

statement: Server-sent events (SSE): a persistent unidirectional channel: the client only establishes the connection, after which the server proactively sends data; the client cannot send anything else. Used when the client has nothing to send (e.g. stock tickers).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you don't need a persistent bi-directional channel, but a persistent unidirectional channel, where your server can send data to the client.

statement: It's 'server-sent events', not 'server-side events'.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: For some reason people call it server-side events. No, it's server-sent events.

statement: SSE examples: stock market tickers; deployment log streaming in CI/CD tools (e.g. Vercel, Netlify) where logs stream into the browser; remote terminals streaming a server process's stdout to the browser.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the deployment log streaming. ... Like Slice, like Vercel, Netlify and whatnot. ... This is also used to build remote terminals.
flags: teacher notes these vendors 'used to leverage it, now they switched their model'

statement: SSE and WebSockets are browser/device-to-server mechanisms; server-to-server use is possible but typically not done because of the overhead.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Server-sent events and WebSockets, they're all browser and device based. ... server to server, people typically don't use it.

statement: SSE is dead simple and very lightweight compared to WebSockets (client subscribes, server sends, client accepts), but you lose bidirectional communication.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it's very lightweight as compared to WebSocket, but you lack bi-directional communication

statement: An SSE implementation takes very few lines: 'hardly 14 lines'; MDN (Mozilla) has a working example of only 21 lines of code.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It hardly takes you 14 lines of code. MDN website ... has a working example which consists of only 21 lines of code

statement: Implement each pattern at least as a hello world (short polling, long polling, WebSocket via Socket.io, SSE via MDN docs); theory alone is jargon (anyone can draw boxes), implementation details make you a better engineer.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: At least write hello world of short polling, long polling, WebSocket, server-sent events.

statement: Medium communication: user -> API server is normal HTTP request/response (over TCP); API server -> database is a persistent plain TCP connection (not a WebSocket).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: From API server to database is a persistent TCP connection. This is not WebSocket.

statement: Medium real-time likes: when two people read the same blog and one claps, the other sees an animation without refreshing; this would be built over WebSocket.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This real-time likes, if you would want to build it, that will happen over WebSocket

statement: Other real-time interactions over WebSocket: Twitter like counts changing live on a celebrity post; hearts on Instagram Live visible to everyone.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When a famous celebrity posts something ... you can see that like count changing on the fly.

statement: Choose based on your use case and understand the trade-offs of every option; write each one to discover its strengths and limits.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: understand the trade-offs of every single thing.

statement: Q: is there a limit on WebSocket connections? A: the limit is physical, same as any TCP connection: they connect on ports, so the same limits apply as with server-to-server TCP connections.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: the limitation is always physical limitation ... because at the end it's TCP.

statement: Q: long polling keeps the connection open until the response, a disadvantage? A: yes. But it is still scalable: it is like a near-persistent connection, similar to WebSocket.
detail: Student concluded long polling isn't scalable; teacher disagreed.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: That's a disadvantage, that your connection is open until you get the response.

statement: You can't replace short polling with long polling everywhere: pick per use case. WebSockets aren't always right (very expensive); short polling may not suit high request surges; long polling works where the wait isn't very long (e.g. 5–10 s).
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: you cannot just replace short polling with long polling in every use case.

statement: Student proposal: for Medium likes, send the like as an HTTP request, update the UI optimistically, and push updated counts via SSE. Teacher: plain SSE doesn't fit since users also send (likes), but 'you can do that'; discuss next week with Slack.
detail: Teacher called the likes box 'a random box' and deferred.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: You can do that. We'll discuss it next week.

statement: Q: in long polling, what if the server goes down? A: the TCP connection breaks; the client must resend. Whether that's safe is use-case specific (fine for cricket scores; payments/e-commerce differ).
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: It's gone. The client has to re-send the request.

statement: Q: should a stock ticker send only a client's watchlist? A: no need: ~10,000 listed companies × 4 bytes = 40,000 bytes ≈ 40 KB per second. Send all; filter on the client.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: 10,000 integers. One integer is 4 bytes. 10,000 into 4, 40,000. 40 KB every second.

statement: Stay away from over-complication; build simple systems.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I stay away from over complication. Like, I like to build simple systems.

statement: SSE can be set up behind a load balancer so backend servers can be scaled (student statement, apparently affirmed).
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: you can set up this SSE over a LB as well
flags: check: "Yes" may be the Teacher answering

statement: Push notifications (GCM, APNs) are entirely different from WebSockets/SSE: different guarantees and protocols, not under your control. You can mimic but not implement them with SSE or periodic checks.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: You can mimic a push notification through server-sent events. But push notifications in itself are totally different.

statement: Calendar apps show meeting push notifications offline because the app raises a local notification for itself, mimicking a push.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: your app itself is generating push notification for your app

statement: Push notifications can also be lost; the difference is their protocol. A persistent connection to GCM always open would be very inefficient, so they use different, optimized specs (GCM differs from APNs).
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: Imagine having a persistent connection open one with GCM always. Very inefficient

statement: In 2015 as a fresher, the teacher's team built a push service natively on GCM and APNs: SNS had terrible delivery rates, OneSignal had just started. That pain is why OneSignal, Twilio etc. now abstract it into an API call.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: SNS did not support good push notifications. They had very, very terrible delivery rates. OneSignal had just started.

statement: Suggested exploration: integrate natively with GCM once using its documentation.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: just try integrating with GCM once natively

statement: Student claimed HTTP's TCP isn't persistent; teacher: it is persistent too, but you explicitly break it after the response.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: No, that is also persistent, but you explicitly break it.

statement: App-to-DB connections don't use WebSockets: each database has its own protocol/dialect over persistent TCP (MySQL, Postgres, MongoDB); e.g. Go code sets SQL dialects.
speaker: student (question)
verbatim: So that is typically called as a dialect, MySQL dialect.

statement: Week 3 goes through the HTTP specification, including why not to use HTTP in certain places.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: in third week, we'll go through HTTP specification

statement: HTTP, WebSocket, SSE each have their own message format; a spec says how to bundle a message so both sides understand.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: HTTP is a format, WebSocket is also format, server-sent event has its own format

statement: Redis has its own spec, RESP; anyone talking to Redis must use that format.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Redis has RESP, which is its own specification.

statement: That covers all six planned components; pre-reads for next week will be shared today.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this is all what I wanted to cover, all the six components. I'll share the pre-reads today

statement: Next week is databases. Saturday: relational databases with a live demo of SQL transactions, locking, concurrency and throughput.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Saturday, we'll take a look at relational databases.

statement: Sunday: NoSQL databases (~1 h), then 1.5–2 h on Slack's real-time communication plus three messaging apps sharing an architecture but differing in guarantees.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the underlying architecture remains the same, while all we change is the guarantees

statement: Video will be uploaded and emailed; Hotmail marks login emails as spam, so use Gmail.
speaker: teacher
